question: Spain’s third deputy prime minister, Teresa Ribera, has hit out at judge Manuel García Castellón on public television, in a clear example of power attacking the judiciary. The judge is following a terrorism case involving fugitive Catalan leader Carles Puigdemont.

The judiciary has come out in defence of the judge and judicial independence, while judges’ associations, along with the General Council of the Judiciary itself, have said that the separation of powers is ‘seriously, critically under threat’.

What is the Commission waiting for to implement the rule of law control mechanism in order to protect Spanish judges from constant populist and partisan attacks by the Catalan Regional Government and the Spanish Government?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.3.2024) The Commission’s 2022 and 2023 Rule of Law Reports1 reported that stakeholders had raised concerns of public statements by politicians, including members of Parliament and the Government, in relation to members of the judiciary.

As reflected in the reports, according to European standards, while courts are not immune to criticism and scrutiny, the judiciary must enjoy public confidence to be successful in view of its special role in society.

This is particularly important in relation to statements by members of the legislative and the executive branches, as all powers of the State must foster and protect the trust of the general public in constitutional institutions including the judiciary.

The Commission remains committed to taking necessary measures to ensure compliance with EU law and upholding the rule of law in all Member States, and will continue to work with the Spanish authorities to promote the rule of law within the framework of the comprehensive rule of law mechanism.
More generally, same as for all the Member States, the Commission follows rule of law developments in Spain under the annual Rule of Law Cycle and its report.
